passage: I'm Sonali, and last month I did something I had never done: I sent out an app before it was ready. I used to dream of two hundred questions, a leaderboard and cartoon levels. Then Seema said in class, "Just show us something." So I put in ten questions and sent the link to eleven classmates. I did not ask anything. I just watched the results. Nearly everyone skipped the two history questions and played all three cricket ones twice. That told me more than any guess of mine. So the next weekend I wrote fifteen more cricket questions and left history alone. I am still a little embarrassed about how plain the first version looked. But I am glad I sent it.

qa.a: The first version had ten questions.

qa.a: Sonali could ask two or three classmates to say aloud what they would change while they play, along with watching which questions get skipped.

qa.q: How might Seema see the app now?
qa.a: Seema, who asked to be shown something, may be pleased to have played it and might like that the cricket topic grew.

Computer teacher's note, Class 9, 12 September
Maria asked to build a quiz app for our class revision instead of the usual poster project. I expected her to spend a month on it.
Instead, she came to me in one week with ten questions, all multiple choice, on science and history. Plain screens, no pictures. She said, "I want to see what people actually use before I make more."
She shared it with twenty classmates and checked the results after two days. Most students skipped the history questions and did the science ones twice. Simran told her the science ones were "like a game".
So she added fifteen more science questions and left history as it was. By the second week, more than thirty students were using it before tests.
I've asked her to show the class how she decided what to build next.

qa.q: How many classmates did Maria first share the quiz with?
qa.a: She shared it with twenty classmates.

qa.q: How might Maria have felt when classmates did the science questions twice?
qa.a: She probably felt encouraged and curious, seeing clearly what people liked and what to build next.

qa.q: What else could Maria try with the history questions, and why?
qa.a: She could ask a few classmates why they skipped them, since changing the format might make history more popular too.

qa.q: How do the classmates experience the quiz app?
qa.a: They find the science questions fun, like a game, and more than thirty use it before tests.

grounding: It shows a teenager releasing a small quiz app with ten questions, watching which ones classmates skip, and adding more of the popular topic.

Saturday
Launched my quiz game for our class today! Well, "launched". It's ten questions on a simple web page I made in computer lab. No sound, no score board, nothing fancy. Seema Didi said to put out something small first and see what people do with it.
I sent the link to the class group at 4. By 9, twenty-two people had played. I could see which questions they finished and which they skipped.
Almost everyone skipped the grammar ones. But the geography map questions? Some people played those three times. Rohan wrote, "Make more of the map ones!!"
So tomorrow I'm going to add ten more map questions and leave grammar alone for now. Maybe next week I'll add a score board, if people keep playing.
I thought building the whole thing would be the hard part. Turns out, watching is more useful.
Nandini

qa.q: How many people had played by 9?
How did Nandini feel about watching which questions people skipped?
qa.a: Nandini felt excited and surprised, finding that watching people was more useful than building everything first.

qa.q: What else could Nandini do before adding the score board?
qa.a: Nandini could check whether people keep playing after the new map questions, so the next feature follows what they actually use.

qa.q: How does Rohan experience the quiz?
qa.a: Rohan enjoys the map questions enough to play them more than once and asks for more.

grounding: It shows a teenager releasing a small ten-question quiz to classmates, noticing which questions they skip, and planning more of the popular topic.
